extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental scientists (readers of Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, performing, and interpreting experiments about the nature of colours and whiteness (prism refraction, reflection, temporal/spatial mixing) to distinguish 'original' vs 'compounded' colours and to produce whiteness by mixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between primary (original) and compounded colours
rubrics_metrics.description: "That colour is primary or original, which cannot by any art be changed, and whose rays are alike refrangible: and that compounded, which is changeable into other colours, and whose rays are not alike refrangible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the refrangibility and changability as the defining test: an original colour's rays are alike refrangible and it resists being altered by mixing; a compounded colour can be transformed into other colours and shows unequal refrangibility. The author emphasizes that some colours which appear simple may themselves be compounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism test for compoundedness (visual test)
rubrics_metrics.description: View the object through a prism: "if it appear confused, and the edges tinged with blue, yellow, or any variety of other colours, then is that ... compounded of such colours as at its edges emerge out of it: but if it appear distinct, and well defined, and entirely [that colour] to the very edges, without any other colours emerging, it is of an original and uncompounded [colour]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a prism to the object or to a refracted beam cast on a white wall. If refraction produces differing colours or the colour changes, conclude the original is compounded; if refractions are uniform and the colour persists unchanged, conclude it is original/uncompounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refraction-of-beams prism test (beam-on-wall variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refract a beam of light, being cast on a white wall, and then interpose another prism; if you find any difformity in the refractions, and the green be transformed into blue, yellow, or varieties, you may conclude that it was compounded; but if the refractions be uniform, and the green persist without any change of colour, then is it original and uncompounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variant uses refracted beams and a second prism to determine whether the rays composing the observed colour are uniform in refrangibility. It also forms part of the argument that uncompounded colours cannot be synthesized by mixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentum Crucis — unequal refrangibility without splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Experimentum Crucis is intended "to show, that rays of divers colours considered apart, do at equal incidences suffer unequal refractions, without being split, rarefied, or any ways dilated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a conceptual/experimental standard: demonstrations should show unequal refrangibility as an inherent property of rays of different colours, not merely as a result of splitting or other hypothesized processes. Experiments should be designed to exclude explanations based on splitting/rarefying of rays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whiteness by rapid temporal succession (rotating wheel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whiteness can be produced by a very quick succession of colours: using "a wheel with many spokes" interposed so half the colours are intercepted by spokes and half pass through interstices; when the wheel is gyrated rapidly so the colours fall in quick succession the resulting colour is a whiteness perfectly like an unrefracted beam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a wheel with equal spokes/interstices sized so different prismatic colours alternately strike the same spot; accelerate rotation until individual colours cannot be distinguished. This demonstrates temporal mixing (persistence of vision) produces white without requiring physical assimilation of rays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whiteness by spatial mixing (reflection from multiple coloured bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place four or five bodies of eminent colours (or a paper painted in several colours in due proportion) in a beam of light so their reflected light falls on a white paper at a convenient distance; when each part of the paper is equally illuminated by all colours, the paper will appear perfectly white.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance is critical: if the paper is too near, its parts show nearest colours; move it back until all parts receive mixed illumination. Intercepting any one colour removes it from the mixture and the white appearance fails. Use prism spectra cast on a wall for convenient, controllable colour sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whiteness by transmissive mixing through coloured glass
rubrics_metrics.description: If no light be admitted into a room but only through coloured glass whose several parts are of several colours in a pretty equal proportion, all white things in the room shall appear white (provided they are not too near the glass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is spatial/transmissive mixing: use transparent colour patches in roughly equal proportions. The persistence of object-colours in the room and in projections through holes is used to argue that rays remain distinct until concourse and that whiteness arises from mixture rather than assimilation of rays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity/luminousness limitation: mixtures may yield grey/dirty white
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflected light from an aggregate of coloured bodies will be much weakened by loss of many rays; "a perfect and intense whiteness is not to be expected, but rather a colour between those of light and shadow, or such a grey or dirty colour as may be made by mixing white and black together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to make whiteness by mixing reflected colours from bulk objects (dust, mixed painter's colours, painted tops), expect diminished intensity and grayer results because not all rays are equally reflected—plan experiments and interpretations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic vs naked-eye observation: apparent whiteness conceals fine structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Many surfaces (froth, painted mixtures, bubbles) that appear white at a distance show distinct individual colours under magnification: "if [froth] be illuminated by reflection from the aforesaid colours, it shall to the naked eye seem white, and yet through a good microscope the several colours will appear distinct on the bubbles."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use microscopic inspection to reveal that apparent whiteness is due to many small coloured reflections whose spatial averaging gives white to the unaided eye. Also, altering visual acuity (straining eyes) can change perception of whiteness vs colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specular transparent fibres reflect colours without changing them (use in classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper's fibres or threads are "transparent and specular; and such substances are known to reflect colours without changing them. To know ... to what species of colour a grey belongs, place any grey body ... and the paper, being illuminated by its reflection, shall appear [colour]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specular reflectors (paper, polished surfaces) as diagnostic tools: the reflected colour indicates the illuminating body's colour. This supports classification of greys/whites and helps distinguish whether a grey is due to mixtures of coloured rays or to diminished luminousness.
